title: Imperfect-work venials: by surprise (semi-voluntary) or smallness of matter
source_text: IX. Rursus vero peccata venialia ex imperfectione operis in duo membra secant. Alia enim ipsis dicuntur venialia ex subreptione; alia ex parvitate materiae. Ex subreptione venialia vocant ea quae non sunt perfecte voluntaria. Quales sunt subiti motus irae, cupiditatis, invidentiae, & alii similes, qui prius in animo existunt, quam ratio plane deliberare potuerit, essent necne admittendi. Quae quidem & peccata sunt, cum praeveniri, aut continuo repelli potuissent, si ratio vigilasset: & tamen venialia sunt, cum pleno voluntatis assensu caruerint. Ex parvitate materiae venialia vocant ea quae in re parva ac levi committuntur. Quale est furtum unius oboli; quod neque proximum notabiliter laedit, neque ejusmodi est, ut apud aequos homines amicitiam tollere queat.
pass_a_gloss: Again, they cut sins venial from the imperfection of the work into two members. For some are called by them venial from surprise; others from smallness of matter. From surprise they call venial those which are not perfectly voluntary. Such are sudden motions of anger, desire, envy, and other like ones, which exist in the mind before reason could fully deliberate whether they ought to be admitted or not. Which indeed are also sins, since they could have been prevented or continually repelled if reason had watched; and yet they are venial, since they lacked the full assent of the will. From smallness of matter they call venial those which are committed in a small and light thing. Such is the theft of a single obol; which neither notably harms the neighbor, nor is of such a kind that it can take away friendship among equitable people.
pass_b_english: Surprise-venials are sudden, not fully deliberate motions—still culpable if reason could have watched, yet not fully willed.
Small-matter venials are light thefts and the like that do not notably wound neighbor or friendship.
